title: Papua New Guinea has about 840 living languages, more than any other country

cover.alt: A misty green valley and forested mountains in the Lower Tari Valley, Hela Province, in the highlands of Papua New Guinea.

body: Ethnologue counts 840 living languages in Papua New Guinea, a country of roughly 12 million people by official estimates, which makes it the most linguistically diverse country in the world; the exact number depends on where you draw the line between a language and a dialect. Most are Papuan languages, alongside Austronesian languages, and the country’s highly mountainous geography kept a scattered rural population apart, so languages multiplied in isolation. To talk across the gaps, people use Tok Pisin, an English-based creole, which with English, Hiri Motu and Papua New Guinean Sign Language is one of four languages with official status.

slides.heading: Language or dialect?
slides.text: The count is not exact. The language catalogue Ethnologue lists 840 living languages; in 2006 the prime minister, Michael Somare, put it at 832 ‘languages, not dialects’. Either way, it is well ahead of any other country.

slides.heading: Four languages with official status
items: Tok Pisin: an English-based creole, the everyday lingua franca
English: government, schools and formal writing
Hiri Motu: read by under 5% of people in 2011
Papua New Guinean Sign Language: official since May 2015

slides.heading: Who could read which language in the 2011 census?
slides.note: Share of people over 10 literate in each language, 2011 census
slides.explanation: Tok Pisin is the most widely read: 68.4% could read it, against 39.9% for English and 4.7% for Hiri Motu.

slides.alt: A sign written in Tok Pisin at the front gate of Lae War Cemetery in Papua New Guinea.
slides.caption: A notice in Tok Pisin, the creole most Papua New Guineans share, at the gate of Lae War Cemetery.

slides.question: What is Tok Pisin?
slides.explanation: Tok Pisin is an English-based creole and the most widely used language in the country. Standard English is used in government, education and formal writing.
